articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls on Friday as Nvidia keeps sliding, but major averages are up for week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls on Friday as Nvidia keeps sliding, but major averages are up for week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite fell on Friday as Nvidia shares added to their recent losses, though the index still headed for a winning week alongside the other two major averages.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 0.9%, while the S&P 500 slid 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline.
Equities initially popped after October's producer price index reading — a measure of wholesale inflation — showed an increase of 0.3% on the month. Economists polled by Dow Jones had seen headline PPI rising 0.4%.
However, the report also showed producer prices gaining 6.5% from 12 months earlier — the biggest annual advance since November 2022.
Nvidia shares weighed on the broader market for another day. The stock fell more than 2% Friday, extending the more than 4% drop it saw in the previous session. The pressure came after the exit of the scandal-hit chipmaker's founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
HSBC downgraded the chipmaker Friday to hold, believing that the stock will languish until the company lays out a permanent succession plan.
Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress , who's worked at the company for more than a decade, will lead the chipmaker as interim CEO. The company's board is looking both internally and externally for a full-time replacement for Huang.
Thomas Martin of Globalt Investments expects the process of finding a new CEO to "take a lot of time" and spur even more uncertainty for the name.
"What will happen to those types of financing arrangements, and will there be less of them just going forward or will there actually be unwinding of them?" the senior portfolio manager told CNBC. "What are the relationships going to be with their suppliers and with their customers? It's just early days."
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all pulled back on Thursday after Huang stepped down from his post following reported extramarital affairs , including a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese spy. Analysts told CNBC that Huang's exit could trigger a 20% correction in the stock.
To be sure, Baird's Ross Mayfield believes a lot of pain has already been priced into the stock, though he still anticipates volatility ahead. More broadly, he expects to see investors continue to rotate into non-AI corners of the market independent of the recent developments with Nvidia.
"Even before all of this came out, and even before the election, chip stocks had been under pressure. There had already been worries about a blue wave — worries about a Democratic sweep — [and] worries about the [return on investment] on all of this capex," the investment strategist said. "It hasn't really changed the broad tenor of the market."
Even with the latest bout of market turbulence, the major averages are heading for weekly advances. The Nasdaq is up about 2%, while the S&P 500 has risen more than 2%. The Dow is poised to post an almost 2% jump. All three indexes are heading for their best weekly performances since early August.
Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is scrambling the tech landscape as investors try to gauge the fallout for chip makers, neoclouds, and others in the artificial intelligence arms race.
The market has quickly passed judgement — bidding up shares of chipmakers like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom while pushing down neoclouds such as Coreweave and AI server maker Dell Technologies .
Traders can benefit from the volatility, but the market has a tendency to overshoot in both directions and estimates are changing rapidly. Long-term investors may want to wait until the dust settles.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
Apple shares climbed nearly 1% Friday, reaching an intraday record of $360.80, lifting the company's market value above $5.2 trillion.
The stock has benefited as investors move away from companies exposed to the AI infrastructure boom.
While many of its Magnificent Seven peers are committed to AI infrastructure buildouts, Apple has managed to stay away from the costly AI arms race. Bernstein analysts recently called Apple a "safe haven " and reiterated an outperform rating on Apple in the report, and a $380 price target, implying about 7% upside from Thursday's close.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making big moves on Friday.
— Darla Mercado and Ananya Chetia
Cisco topped estimates on fiscal first-quarter earnings on Thursday, but Wall Street analysts are still somewhat measured on the outlook for the make of networking technologies amid the AI boom.
Tim Long at Barclays maintained his equal-weight rating on the stock in a Friday note, with a price target of $109 and potential upside of 6.9%.
"One area of weakness in the quarter was that hyperscaler AI orders were likely down meaningfully Q/Q in FQ1 based on our estimates, but these orders tend to be lumpy," he said.
Michael Ng at Goldman Sachs has a neutral rating on the stock, noting an "orders miss," per a Nov. 12 note.
"The margin outlook and upgrade was better-than-expected with CSCO demonstrating strong operating leverage, though growing hyperscale revenue mix may be headwinds to gross margin in F2H27," he said.
Nvidia is going to struggle until it gets a new CEO to permanently replace Jensen Huang and take over from CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress, according to HSBC.
Analyst Frank Lee downgraded the chipmaker to hold from buy. His price target of $170, down from $365, implies upside of just 2.3% from Thursday's close.
"We believe the uncertainties will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out and the new CEO is able to demonstrate execution capabilities," Lee said in a Friday note to clients.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Bitcoin traded below $70,000 for the first time since August in a risk-off move, falling as low as $67,632.68, its lowest level since Aug. 19, according to Coin Metrics.
Its recent weakness coincides with strength in the U.S. dollar. On Friday, the dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold – despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling and, this week, more than $1 billion in leveraged bitcoin liquidations, per CoinGlass. The declines began in late October, as concerns over AI valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off, and were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite gave up their early gains and moved into negative territory in morning trading on Friday.
The broad market index was down 0.4%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 0.7%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average , however, rose 43 points, or 0.1%.
The three major averages began Friday's session in the green

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang was a ‘China salesman’ for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang was a ‘China salesman’ for Nvidia. His exit is weighing on Chinese tech stocks.
articles.content_orig:

The CEO of the world’s second most valuable company in the world has stepped down amid a sex and spying scandal, and President Donald Trump, who shared a relationship with the ousted tech titan, is now telling the world who he thinks should replace him.
Writing on Truth Social , Trump said that “only one man” — former Apple CEO Tim Cook — could take the place of now-former Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post on Thursday after the tech giant was rocked by reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy .
Trump added that a decision by Nvidia’s board to name Cook, whom Trump once mistakenly referred to as “Tim Apple,” as Huang’s successor would mean “a Legend replaces a Legend.”
Cook, 66, served as Apple’s chief operating officer from 2005 until he was elevated to be the company’s CEO after the death of co-founder Steve Jobs. He stepped down as Apple’s CEO earlier this year but has remained the company’s executive chairman.
Huang’s resignation came on Thursday amid a scandal that has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off the chipmaker’s market value, with share prices plunging 10 percent Thursday morning.
His troubles began last week when The New York Times reported that he’d carried on a long affair with another technology executive named Alice Huang, who American intelligence officials believe is either an agent or asset of China’s Ministry of State Security — Beijing’s equivalent of the Central Intelligence Agency.
Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is believed to have facilitated shipments of Nvidia’s microchips to Chinese firms in violation of U.S. export controls as part of a foreign intelligence operation. Beijing has denied the claims of espionage as“purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
The Times subsequently reported that Mr Huang had also had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell , his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
After the first of the infidelities was disclosed, the executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years, Lori Huang, and said he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had case without going into details.
Nvidia’s board responded by launching an internal investigation led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
The scandal involving the two Huangs has raised alarms among Democrats and some Republicans who have questioned what Trump knew about Jensen Huang’s behavior, whether it threatened American national security, and whether Trump and others in his administration turned a blind eye to the entire matter rather than risk destabilizing a company that has played a large part in propping up the American stock market in spite of Trump administration policies that have caused widespread economic chaos and increased the cost of living for millions of Americans.
Since Trump’s return to the White House last year, both Cook and Huang have cozied up to the 80-year-old president in conspicuous fashion, with both appearing at a state dinner honoring China’s Xi Jinping in September.
Huang has been particularly cozy with Trump as he and his administration have gone all-in on pushing to grow the American Artificial Intelligence sector to counter China’s burgeoning AI efforts, even as the Trump administration has relaxed export controls on top-end AI chips produced by Nvidia.
During a trip to China earlier this year, Trump had Air Force One make an extended stop at an Alaska air base so Huang, who’d flown there aboard his own private jet, could join the presidential party en route to Beijing.
The inclusion of Huang as a surprise passenger aboard Air Force One came after Trump had been briefed by top officials — including his Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio — on the Nvidia CEO’s involvement with the alleged MSS asset .
Earlier this week Trump said he had “absolutely no idea” that the first reported affair was with a suspected Chinese spy.
“I think ​he's an honorable guy," Trump told reporters, adding ​that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country”.
Republican leaders of three House committees have meanwhile called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset.
And Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have written to Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.
Joe Sommerlad contributed reporting from London

articles.title_orig: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
articles.title_zh: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers.
Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday.
Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning.
In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online.
In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing.
Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.
Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete.
The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.
Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday.
Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.
The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.
Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.
U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress.
"Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said.
Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.
Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.
A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more.
Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.
The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.
"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."
"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.
Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.
"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

articles.title_orig: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Nvidia continued to slide after the market open on Friday after declining 4% on Thursday following news of co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, amid reports about his personal relationships and national security concerns. The news has raised questions for investors about what comes next for a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.
To gauge how wealth managers are responding, CNBC polled members of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council. Thirty of the 122 firms and professionals contacted responded to the online, multiple-choice flash poll, conducted between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. The poll is a snapshot of respondents' views, not a measure of all financial advisors.
Most respondents, 19, said they are holding their Nvidia positions steady. Another four said they are increasing their stake, while seven said they do not own the stock. None said they were selling at the time of the poll.
"Most of our clients are in a position to hold; the reason is because it makes up a smaller percentage of an overall diversified portfolio," Winnie Sun , managing director and founding partner of Irvine, California-based Sun Group Wealth Partners, said in an interview. Sun is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council.
Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:
In open responses, several advisors wrote that they are taking a "wait-and-see" approach before changing their investment strategy with Nvidia and are telling their clients to do the same.
"Don't react to short-term headlines," wrote certified financial planner Peyton Jamison, president of Jamison Private Wealth Management in Alpharetta, Georgia. "The company's valuation is extremely attractive, and the focus should remain on its underlying fundamentals and long-term investment potential." His firm is ranked No. 78 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.
Asked what factors could change their approach to Nvidia, 13 respondents cited the outlook for AI demand, 11 pointed to valuation, and 10 mentioned company leadership or governance. Some said the decision depends on the client, with eight citing risk tolerance and seven mentioning portfolio concentration. Seven said they do not expect to change their approach.
Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results Tuesday, after the market close. In poll remarks, advisors said the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings will help determine their course of action.
Advisors said that for investors, what to do may depend on how much Nvidia stock they already own, when they expect to need the money and how comfortable they are with volatility.
"If this is a company that's going to keep you up at night and you just feel really uncomfortable with these unknown risks, then there was always the option to sell and move that capital to another stock or another portfolio," Sun said.
Nvidia exposure can also come through mutual funds and ETFs . Nvidia's large market value makes it a significant holding in many broad-market funds, including funds that track the S&P 500, as well as target-date funds in retirement-plan options.
Investors can check their Nvidia exposure by reviewing the fact sheets for the funds in their 401(k) or brokerage accounts, which typically list a fund's largest holdings. A stock's decline does not translate one-for-one into a fund's decline.
However, investors with dedicated technology, semiconductor or growth funds may have more Nvidia exposure than they realize, advisors say.
"Nvidia is a big part of virtually everyone's portfolio whether they take an active or passive index approach," wrote Andy Pratt, a partner and director of investment strategy at Burney Wealth Management in Reston, Virginia, which is ranked No. 34 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.
He said he advises clients not to overreact to short-term news and to let the dust settle before making decisions.
— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

articles.title_orig: Two top Trump Cabinet officials go to war over China spy scandal amid explosive accusations: report
articles.title_zh: Two top Trump Cabinet officials go to war over China spy scandal amid explosive accusations: report
articles.content_orig:
The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses Melania Trump's diplomatic efforts, including brokering a temporary limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
First lady Melania Trump and envoys from both Russia and Ukraine spoke from the White House on Thursday, hailing the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Oleshky region as a potential "spark" for peace that lasts beyond a temporary regional ceasefire.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said in a White House trilateral news conference with the two warring countries. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."
"Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire," she added, calling Oleshky "a spark in a world of darkness capable of illuminating the best in humanity."
INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL
Trump said she became aware of a humanitarian crisis in the region in September and directed her representative, Marc Beckman, to engage with Russia and Ukraine on her behalf. She said both countries agreed to work with her as an "exclusive intermediary" to establish a ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region, deliver humanitarian aid and create a safe evacuation route for civilians.
Her remarks were followed by comments from Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev , who said Russian President Vladimir Putin appreciated President Donald Trump’s efforts to stop the fighting.
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS
Leader of the Servant of the People political party of Ukraine, David Arakhamia, sitting side by side with Russia's presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev was a unique image at first lady Melania Trump's remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 5, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
"President Putin also appreciates President Trump's peacemaking effort and his team working on a peace plan to resolve Ukrainian crisis," Dmitriev said in a rare moment of a Russian diplomat speaking at the White House. "President Trump has asked President Putin to support a number of initiatives on exchanging of prisoners, on releasing U.S. prisoners on humanitarian efforts. And President Putin supported those ideas and those initiatives."
"And it's very important that cooperation between Russia and Ukraine and Russia in the United States matters not only for our two nations, but for the entire world," he continued. "Let us continue making great humanitarian contributions. We can together, let us build a future of peace, partnership and prosperity for the benefit of our families, our children and future generations."
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN
First lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
"Dear Melania, you saved and touched so many lives," he concluded.
David Arakhamia, the leader of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's political party, called Melania Trump's ceasefire the 'biggest de-escalation since 2022," when the war began.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA
"Madam first lady, I would like to thank you: You did an amazing job," he said. "I think when everything started with you and your team, we had about 5% of people who believed in success, and 95% of skeptics who said it wasn’t going to work. Now, after it happened, it’s switched completely: 95% of the people believe that we can do things like that, and 5% are still skeptical."
Peace is now a matter of when, not if, he added.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
Signature page from Oleshky ceasefire agreement. (Provided to Fox News Digital)
Getting fearful Ukrainians out of the Russian-controlled city is an important step toward deciding how peace will be made and determining the long-term fate of the occupied territory of southern Ukraine.
"On the first day, people in the area did not believe it was happening," Arakhamia said. "They stayed in their homes, waiting to see if the clock was ticking backward. The next day, they started walking around their homes. The day after that, they came to see their broken homes and find their belongings.
"This is really emotional to watch and supervise, to understand what we are doing," he added. "I think we are creating momentum where both sides are learning the little mechanics of how to keep the peace when the peace comes.
"I would also like to sincerely thank you, from my heart, for doing this."

Dmitriev attended the event and met with U.S. officials, sources told Reuters. Dmytro Lubinets , Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, also attended the event.

articles.title_orig: The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone
articles.title_zh: The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone
articles.content_orig:
On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.
The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.
While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more new climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.
In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.
While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.
“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.
Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.
Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”
But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.
“We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”
It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.
“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”
Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.content_orig:
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.
That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.
And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.
But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?
Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.
However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.
In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.
Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.
“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.
“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.
“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.
That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.
On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.
According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.
The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.
Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.
The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.
There would be serious divisions.
“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.
But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.
Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.
“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.
Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”
“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.
Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.
“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.
But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.
Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.
In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.
While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister .
Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly , killing about 1,400 Palestinians.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine updates: Russia hit with second car bomb attack in two days
articles.title_zh: Ukraine updates: Russia hit with second car bomb attack in two days
articles.content_orig:
Here are the latest developments from the Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, November 13:
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday directly contradicted US envoy Jared Kushner's Thursday statement that President Vladimir Putin had voiced willingness to have European representatives join upcoming talks designed to end his war of aggression against Ukraine.
Responding to a request for comment from Germany's DPA news agency, Zakharova said, "As far as Russia's Foreign Ministry is aware, the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."
No Foreign Ministry representatives were present during a Thursday meeting between Putin and US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff according to Russian state media, which said Putin was accompanied by his own foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday said the EU will take part in future peace talks aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and will jointly represent Europe with France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK .
"Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussion that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort," Costa said after a European leaders' meeting in Dublin.
European and Ukrainian leaders have long insisted on the format, while Russia has rejected the idea and the US appeared indifferent under the Trump administration.
The situation appears to have changed slightly, with US envoy and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner saying late Thursday, "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin "is willing to give it a try."
Despite consensus about wanting peace after nearly five years of Russia's war of aggression, Europe lacks unanimity as to who should be representing the interests of the continent and member states.
Russia and the US have called for one single representative to be present, whereas several nations have called for a diplomatic team.
The question of who will represent the EU itself remains unresolved.
The bloc's foreign affairs boss Kaja Kallas — a staunch critic of Russia and its war — said Friday, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." Adding, "I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?"
With frustration growing over Russian aggression on Europe's doorstep, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs put things in perspective. Pointing to the fact that Europe is more populous, richer and more militarily powerful than Russia, he said Friday, "We as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no clear explanations have been given for recent speed issues with Starshield.
The Ukrainian president said on Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.
Zelenskyy doubled down on his comments on Friday, saying the issue remained unsolved.
He said the connections were only working when devices were moving slower than 161 kilometres (100 miles) per hour.
"This makes it impossible, in particular, to use interceptors against jet-powered 'Shaheds.'" he added. The Ukrainian president also said he instructed his ministers to step up contacts with the US side.
The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.
Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."
Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with the Russian President Vladimir Putin .
Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week.
Speaking on the sidelines of the European Union meetings in Dublin, Merz said that "some here ⁠in ⁠fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'."
The Russian and US presidents held talks in Anchorage, Alaska, last summer, the outcome of which European side views as favoring Putin.
"I ‌therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," Merz said.
He also stated that Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia .
"Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," he said.
Merz also said it was a "given" that his country would involved in the next round of Ukraine talks.
Kyiv residents are bracing for another difficult winter as Russian airstrikes continue to target the Ukrainian capital’s energy infrastructure. Long and unpredictable power and water outages are disrupting daily life, forcing families to rely on batteries, portable power stations and improvised routines.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.
When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.
The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi , followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy .
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.
Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine , alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
Read more about the uncertainty over Europe’s representation in the Ukraine peace talks
Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.
US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​ Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.
"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.
"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

articles.title_orig: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models—uh oh, Jensen!
articles.title_zh: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models—uh oh, Jensen!
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.
The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China's intelligence service.
While Jensen Huang's relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia's potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.
U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country's leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.
Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot's Kimi's K3 releases and DeepSeek's V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.
White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.
That doesn't mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch's data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.
However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.
"If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn't make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want," Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.
Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and Singaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.
In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a " China problem " because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed's relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang's companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.
Ironically, short-seller Culper's bet against Nvidia wasn't driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government's response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.
If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven't been cleared for import.
Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn't buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.
For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang's personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed's data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.
The U.S. government's treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that licensing chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
articles.title_zh: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
articles.content_orig:
In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.
The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.
"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.
Yet the firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.
The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, according to Axios .
By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to Axios, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.
Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.
Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.
An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.
Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."
"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.
There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.
"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.
Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick and his sons did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.
As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.
Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.
But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the Departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."
Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy . At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing .
That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing , as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China .
Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026 , with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.
Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.
"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to non-public government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.
The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.
Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30 , the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.
Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.
Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured , a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.
As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to Axios, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show .
On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.
"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.
Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.
Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, Axios reported.
On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor w

articles.title_orig: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei aims to 'underpromise and overdeliver' as IPO valuation drops below $2T hopes
articles.title_zh: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei aims to 'underpromise and overdeliver' as IPO valuation drops below $2T hopes
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A future of new scientific discovery where cancer, Alzheimer's, and heart disease are considered relics of the past, and artificial intelligence agents perform a growing number of complex tasks for humans safely.
Those were among the ambitions Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei laid out to JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) CEO Jamie Dimon Friday as the artificial intelligence startup prepares for one of the largest initial public offerings in history.
"We can have a much more beautiful world… It sounds starry-eyed. It sounds crazy. I really do believe it," Amodei said.
The remarks came during a livestreamed conversation hosted at JPMorgan's Manhattan headquarters, one of Anthropic's final stops this week in its Wall Street push to drum up investor demand for its IPO next week.
Amodei laid out a sweeping vision for the technology, from accelerating scientific discoveries and transforming medicine to deploying increasingly capable AI agents in fields such as robotics and cybersecurity.
He also pointed to the company's technology creating new markets.
"You're on an exponential of cognition, and as the exponential proceeds, new markets become possible," Amodei told Dimon.
But realizing those ambitions comes with enormous financial costs. Amodei described securing enough computing power to support Anthropic's growth without spending beyond its means as the company's "deepest business dilemma."
Asked by Dimon why Anthropic is going public now, the Princeton PhD pointed to the need for additional cash to help manage the uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's computing investments.
The company must commit to expensive infrastructure well before it knows how much demand its AI products will generate. Amodei said Anthropic generally purchases less capacity in advance than its growth projections might justify, supplementing it when demand exceeds expectations.
"We actually tend to buy on the low side," he said.
The IPO would provide an additional financial cushion as Anthropic balances those risks against its extraordinary growth ambitions.
"Just the more cash we have on hand, the more buffer we have between those two things," Amodei said, while suggesting the company isn't seeking to secure its highest valuation possible.
Anthropic wants to "underpromise and overdeliver," Amodei said.
Anthropic expects to price its offering Wednesday and begin trading Thursday, Nov. 19 , seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion through its IPO and a concurrent private share sale at a valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion, according to the company's IPO website .
Just weeks ago, investors anticipated the company seeking a valuation as high as $2 trillion. Headwinds to financial conditions for the massive offering have been mounting in recent weeks as borrowing costs have climbed, political backlash over US data center development has won midterm election voters, and turmoil swirls around one of Anthropic's biggest chip suppliers and investors, Nvidia ( NVDA ).
In its IPO roadshow video earlier this week, Anthropic emphasized the durability of its revenue growth and its ability to use its own Claude technology to improve efficiency and control costs.
Anthropic has tapped JPMorgan to lead US retail sales in its IPO. Along with lead underwriting banks Goldman Sachs ( GS ) and Morgan Stanley ( MS ), it's one of 19 Wall Street lenders helping the company go public.
Evercore analysts estimated on Wednesday that the banks could earn roughly $395 million from the IPO, with JPMorgan taking home about $44 million in fees or about 0.1% of its fourth quarter earnings per share. That compares to $75 million in underwriting fees JPMorgan earned helping SpaceX go public.

articles.title_orig: China’s Military Purges Accelerate
articles.title_zh: China’s Military Purges Accelerate
articles.content_orig:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.
Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.
General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.
“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.
Three officials in Taiwan said they believed Mr. Xi’s loyalty campaign would keep the Chinese military focused on its own problems. That could hinder preparations for possible war over Taiwan, the self-governed island democracy that Beijing claims. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal assessments.
The leadership uncertainty comes as China’s military has continued to pressure Taiwan. Dozens of P.L.A. ships held unannounced drills in seas off the Chinese coast in recent weeks, with some, including a carrier strike group, still remaining, Joseph Wu , the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, posted on X on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: US producer prices rise moderately in October, but inflation broadens out
articles.title_zh: US producer prices rise moderately in October, but inflation broadens out
articles.content_orig:
High energy prices continue to ripple through US supply chains, raising the costs for businesses and setting the stage for further increases in the coming months for American consumers.
Wholesale inflation accelerated last month to its highest rate in nearly four years, Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed Friday.
The Producer Price Index, a measurement of average price changes received by producers and manufacturers, rose 0.3% from the month before and 6.5% for the 12 months ended in October, the highest annual rate since November 2022.
Excluding gas and food prices, core PPI rose 0.3% on a monthly basis and 5% annually, matching a rate last seen in January 2023.
The Iran war and the resulting energy supply shock have sent gas and diesel prices markedly higher in recent months.
Fuel prices didn’t rise as quickly last month as they did in September (when PPI rose at a breakneck rate of 1.4% to reach 6.3%); however, the past months’ surge, coupled with other more persistent price pressures, kept wholesale inflation quite elevated.
Notably, food prices climbed rapidly higher for the second consecutive month, rising 1.3% in October – the fastest monthly hike since July 2022 – after increasing 1.1% in September.
Within food, the largest price spikes were seen for produce products, which are primarily transported via truck . Freight transportation costs for the trucking industry are up nearly 25% from last year, BLS data shows.
Friday’s report showed that prices for wholesale fresh and dry vegetables jumped 26.7% in October, following a 30.7% leap in September.
The high diesel costs continue to flow to other categories, lifting costs for transportation, warehousing and key inputs like chemicals.
While PPI doesn’t translate directly to the Consumer Price Index, its trajectory and category-specific price hikes can serve as a potential bellwether for what consumers could experience in near future.
“We’ve seen a lot of pass-through already in places like airfares, where consumer prices have risen a lot,” Matt Bush, US economist at Guggenheim Investments, told CNN in an interview.
However, the higher transportation and input costs businesses are seeing now might not hit consumers for another six to eight months, he said.
“And it’s complicated by the fact that we also have some lingering tariff effects on a lot of these consumer goods prices,” he said.
As a result, consumers could be in store for further sticker shock early next year.
“That’s when the majority of businesses do their annual price resets,” he said. “In the case of the energy shock, there was an expectation that it could be short-lived; but given it’s gone on for several months now, I think as we head into the new year that you will see a lot of businesses deciding they need to pass on at least some of these costs.”
At the same time, the massive investment in artificial intelligence technology and equipment are contributing another layer of inflationary pressures both for businesses and consumers.
Electronic components and accessories, which rose at a six-month high pace of 4.2%, are up 31.7% from the year before, the highest annual rate on record, according to BLS data that goes back to December 1966.
“Those don’t pass through as directly into consumer prices; but indirectly, we are seeing it show up in computer prices, TV prices, software prices,” Bush said.
Explaining inflation’s impact on the midterms
Friday’s PPI data, coupled with the hotter-than-expected October CPI released earlier this week, are expected to result in a rate hike from the Federal Reserve when policymakers meet in early December.
Markets are expecting a quarter-point hike; however, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated earlier this week that a half-point hike could be necessary.
The rate hikes might not end with December, said Ben Ayers, Nationwide senior economist.
“Lingering impacts from the spike in fuel prices could linger into 2027, warranting further tightening by the Fed to limit second and third order inflation impacts,” he wrote in a note Friday.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Falls. It Faces One Big Threat in Life After Jensen.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Falls. It Faces One Big Threat in Life After Jensen.
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slumped on Friday, led by the chip makers caught in the swirl of Nvidia’s leadership turmoil, at the end of another volatile week for the market that, nonetheless, remained on course for its best week in months.
The S&P 500 is on track to rise roughly 2 percent for the week, which would be its best weekly performance since early August. That would come despite a 0.7 percent decline on Friday, capping a week that swung from gains to losses and back multiple times.
The Nasdaq Composite is up roughly 1.5 percent for the week, even after a fall on Friday.
The moves mark an end to weeks of losses in which concerns about a slowdown in the growth of the artificial intelligence industry weighed on the market and prompted sharp sell-offs in many of the tech companies that have led the market higher in recent years.
Friday’s sell-off, however, underscored earlier analyst warnings of the likelihood of more volatility to come, even if many still expect the market to rally through the end of the year.
“The market is in an incredibly good position to move higher,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for the investment management arm at Nationwide, an insurance company. “Once you get through the news-driven sentiment, you can get back to focusing on fundamentals. That is hopefully what we are seeing.”
The market was on edge after revelations that Mr. Huang, a standard-bearer for the A.I. revolution , had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

articles.title_orig: In China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism
articles.title_zh: In China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.
Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.
Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."
Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.
There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.
Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.
Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.
