articles.title_orig: Before he was Pope Leo, he was their bishop. Now he’s back home.
articles.title_zh: Before he was Pope Leo, he was their bishop. Now he’s back home.
articles.content_orig:
LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV made a triumphant return Friday to the Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for eight years and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto.”
Leo arrived in a plane decorated with “#LeoXFliesHome” stickers and he was greeted with a sign at the airport bearing the same message. A small dance troupe performed before him as he stepped off the plane.
He will stay in the area until Sunday to lead eight events, including a private dinner with the priests who once reported to him as bishop.
The crowds greeting Leo in Peru’s fourth largest city will likely be smaller than the estimated 3 million or so who welcomed the pope when he arrived Wednesday in Lima, the country’s capital.
But their enthusiasm more than made up for their smaller numbers as the former Bishop Robert Prevost of Chiclayo returned to this coastal city of nearly 700,000 as the leader of the  Catholic Church.
As toured in an open-air popemobile at the Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert plain just outside Chiclayo, the crowd erupted in cheers, many waving waved white-and-yellow Vatican flags.
Some had been waiting since last night to catch a glimpse of the pontiff, many of them forced to walk as lines of cars had blocked the roads where vendors sold hats, mini pope dolls and sweet Peruvian bread.
Maria Esther Chozo Reyes, 76, said she had taken a 12-hour bus ride from Lima and arrived Thursday afternoon before she camped overnight. “He knows the people of Chiclayo and he’s lived here, he’s made his mission here,” she told The Associated Press. “We really need his blessing.”
Thanking the people for their love and support, in his sermon Leo said it was a blessing to be in his former home.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer ⁠of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said, adding that his lung cancer disgnosis and surgery to remove part of one lung exactly a month ago had been a time of trial.
Leo’s sojourn to Chiclayo is midway through the final leg of his 12-day visit to South America , a historic trip that included stops in Argentina and Uruguay. And it’s the most sentimental part of his journey.
For while Leo was born in Chicago and English is his mother tongue, the first words he uttered from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica was a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved Diocese of Chiclayo.”
During his time in that city, Leo often repeated a joke: “Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter.”
Setting aside the fact that it’s actually two letters, Leo quickly became a beloved figure in Chiclayo by championing social justice issues, embracing the poor and venturing into the local prison to say Mass.
During the pandemic, Leo endeared himself to many by launching a fundraising drive to raise money for a badly-needed oxygen production plant.
When Cyclone Maku hit the area in March 2023, Leo was photographed wading through the floodwaters to get supplies to the destitute and distributing food at soup kitchens.
At Christmastime, Leo would drive a pickup truck laden with gifts into remote villages around Chiclayo and join family celebrations.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary, priest and finally as a bishop in Peru and became a citizen in 2015. During his two decades in the country, he was also a strident critic of then- Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori’s authoritarian regime .
On Thursday, Leo delivered a speech while sitting beside Fujimori’s daughter, recently-elected Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional performing arts center.
Leo urged the country’s leaders to cultivate honesty and integrity to strengthen public trust --- and called on officeholders to listen to their constituents.
“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said.
There was thunderous applause when Leo referred to Peru as “my homeland.”
And Leo appeared to have tears in his eyes as he sang the Peruvian national anthem along with a children’s choir.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Lima and Corky Siemaszko from New York.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.
OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022. OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute who had previously heard about OpenAI’s reorganization, told Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work. OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models. The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.
This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.
But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.
Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.
Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.
Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.
“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots.
Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer.
Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Lost His Job. Wall Street Lost Its Biggest Prize.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Lost His Job. Wall Street Lost Its Biggest Prize.
articles.content_orig:
With Jensen Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia, Wall Street has lost its most powerful and profitable dealmaker.
As Mr. Huang built Nvidia from a regional chipmaker into the world’s largest company, he dispensed with the usual careful, corporate hand-wringing. He personally directed splashy deals and complicated financing structures that pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into would-be competitors, suppliers and customers.
If that made him, in the public eye, a face of the global A.I. build out, on Wall Street he represented something else: manna. His deals produced billions of dollars in fees for banks, asset managers and advisers, and Nvidia was, up until this week, spending or promising money at a speed and magnitude of little precedence.
Now Wall Street bankers, traders and even some of Nvidia’s competitors are wondering and worrying about whether Mr. Huang’s departure will slow the breakneck pace of Nvidia’s investments.
Some say that the fundamentals of Nvidia’s power are still intact, like its extreme control of the global supply of chips, the A.I. boom’s scarcest resource, the company’s deep cash coffers and the Trump administration’s warm support for the industry’s regulatory agenda. But Mr. Huang was the leader who harnessed all of those assets into a deal-making machine.
“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I.,” said Michael Edwards, director of Forum Markets, an A.I.-focused merchant bank. “Imagine the Fed without a chairman.”

articles.title_orig: Arm boss Rene Haas approached in Nvidia CEO search
articles.title_zh: Arm boss Rene Haas approached in Nvidia CEO search
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia hasn't yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang , the company's board told CNBC.
"We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role," the board said in a Friday statement. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates."
The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy.
Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Kress conducted her first meeting as interim CEO on Thursday afternoon with high-level executives at Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal details.
The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang's successor, citing people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia's board said, "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature."
Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business.
Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company's market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang's departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct.
On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.
Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for briefings, and renewed those calls even after the CEO's resignation. The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss "serious concerns about our national security," and how the company's top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China.

articles.title_orig: After 3 Weeks and More Than 451,000 Folds, the iPhone Duo's Hinge Is Finally Starting to Fail
articles.title_zh: After 3 Weeks and More Than 451,000 Folds, the iPhone Duo's Hinge Is Finally Starting to Fail
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Three weeks ago, we put Apple’s new iPhone Duo on our custom foldable phone testing rig, the Fold-a-Phone , to find out how many times it could fold until it broke. It’s not fully broken yet, but the hinge has started to break down.
I initially detected some looseness in the hinge motion yesterday during our afternoon livestream . It became evident that the iPhone Duo was not opening with the same firm sound I was used to hearing. When I left the office last night at 6 p.m., it was still opening completely flat.
Now, however, the screen no longer opens all the way flat. Instead, it unfolds most of the way but leaves a few degrees of angle in the hinge. Check out the video below to see for yourself.
After examining the sensor data we’ve collected, and the photos and videos we shoot constantly during the testing process, we determined that changes in the opening force and motion began occurring around the 390,000-fold point on Tuesday afternoon and gradually built until last night.
The wire we use to open the phone screen would withdraw before the screen was in the fully open position, but it would then sort of “coast” the rest of the way down. But between 12:30 and 1 a.m. this morning, around 440,300 folds, the screen would no longer have time to open all the way before the Fold-a-Phone caused it to close again.
How serious is this issue? In the grand scheme of things, not very. The phone still operates and maintains other screen positions without issue. There’s no cracking, signs of a more visible crease or other failures.
This issue is not sufficient to meet our established failure conditions in the Duo, which include loss of power, sensors failing to detect the screen where it needs to be within the given timeframe, and screen blackout. The phone is only about 5 to 10 degrees away from the fully open state, and it can still be moved the rest of the way by hand (though without the distinctive snap sound and feel it had earlier).
Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.
Chances are, if you had bought the phone and encountered this behavior, you might not even notice it at first. And, remember, by the time this started, we’d subjected the iPhone Duo to the equivalent of nearly 12 and a half years of folding (assuming 100 folds per day) – well beyond the number of folds we’d expect from even an avid user.
Apple has not publicly stated the anticipated number of folds the iPhone Duo would endure, so we’ve been left to speculate. Guesses within CNET have ranged from 500,000 (matching Samsung’s rating for the Galaxy Z Fold 8) to 1.5 million. But even if we don’t yet know for sure how much worse the hinge action will become, and thus what the final number will be, what we’ve seen today represents the first significant step toward failure.
We are going to keep going. And we hope you’ll stick with us, both here and on our daily livestreams, to see what more unfolds.

articles.title_orig: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Our proposals were almost laughed at.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title_orig: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.title_zh: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.content_orig:
The 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index , a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected.
The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 3 basis points to 5.133%. It reached a high of 5.174% earlier in the day.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by less than 1 basis point at 4.855%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was 4 basis points higher at 5.47%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
October's producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022.
There was "no silver lining" in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes  food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October.
"It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation," he said.
The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday's session , with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 86%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%.
Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil set for its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. Prices were choppy in early trading Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.3% at $96.11.

articles.title_orig: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.title_zh: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.content_orig:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.
On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.
By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.
Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.
“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote . “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”
What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.
Nightmare Eclipse said the exploit worked against Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. People can see if their systems are vulnerable by checking the CLFS authentication mode. If it’s in learning mode or enforcement mode, the system is vulnerable, and the PoC supplied in the post should spawn a SYSTEM shell. Nightmare Eclipse has published numerous other Windows zero-days in recent months.
Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there’s a catch, he said.
“The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems,” he explained. “That is, you can’t just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work.”
For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1.” Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement.
Microsoft does staged rollouts of Windows updates, such as 26H2, so it’s not clear how many people have it. You can check by running the “winver” command. In a statement sent after this post went live, Microsoft said it was investigating the writeup and had no evidence the vulnerability was being exploited in the wild. The company also said Defender blocks potential exploitation attempts.
This story was updated to add Microsoft’s comment.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s stock is on a losing streak not seen in 14 years. What comes next?
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s stock is on a losing streak not seen in 14 years. What comes next?
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slumped on Friday, led by the chip makers caught in the swirl of Nvidia’s leadership turmoil, at the end of another volatile week for the market that, nonetheless, remained on course for its best week in months.
The S&P 500 is on track to rise roughly 2 percent for the week, which would be its best weekly performance since early August. That would come despite a 0.7 percent decline on Friday, capping a week that swung from gains to losses and back multiple times.
The Nasdaq Composite is up roughly 1.5 percent for the week, even after a fall on Friday.
The moves mark an end to weeks of losses in which concerns about a slowdown in the growth of the artificial intelligence industry weighed on the market and prompted sharp sell-offs in many of the tech companies that have led the market higher in recent years.
Friday’s sell-off, however, underscored earlier analyst warnings of the likelihood of more volatility to come, even if many still expect the market to rally through the end of the year.
“The market is in an incredibly good position to move higher,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for the investment management arm at Nationwide, an insurance company. “Once you get through the news-driven sentiment, you can get back to focusing on fundamentals. That is hopefully what we are seeing.”
The market was on edge after revelations that Mr. Huang, a standard-bearer for the A.I. revolution , had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

articles.title_orig: Police investigating David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences
articles.title_zh: Police investigating David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences
articles.content_orig:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".
It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.
The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".
When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".
"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.
Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.
"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."
Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.
Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.
One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.
He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.
The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.
The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.
Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.
In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.
"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

articles.title_orig: What Vladimir Putin won in Abu Dhabi Ukraine peace talks
articles.title_zh: What Vladimir Putin won in Abu Dhabi Ukraine peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.
The Russians surely must be stoked with the outcome of the latest round of U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. In the United Arab Emirates, Donald Trump’s envoys endorsed the Kremlin’s long-standing demand for everything to be negotiated in one fell swoop.
And the U.S. president subsequently raised the prospect of a “very big” deal involving all of Europe.
The ambitious aim apparently now agreed between Washington and Moscow is to discuss all the issues together. And then to “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time,” Jared Kushner explained to reporters in a post-talks briefing in the UAE’s capital. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was representing the U.S. in the talks, along with Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor who is Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East.
So much for sequencing — generally seen by experienced diplomatic negotiators as crucial to any successful peace talks. And so much, too, for starting with a ceasefire or the tiresome breaking down of complex issues into discrete and manageable tasks to try to move things along while raising confidence and inspiring trust.
To be sure, Russia and the United States won’t be able to strike a deal on their own. Ukraine will get a say, and European leaders have already pushed back against Trump’s big, beautiful deal, rejecting any attempt by the White House and the Kremlin to reshape the continent’s security architecture.
But it has been a longstanding Kremlin goal to get the U.S. to agree to the “let’s talk about everything” strategy, a process that will succeed in “diverting attention from what really is the critical issue, and that’s the war on Ukraine,” said Eugene Rumer, who served on the U.S. National Intelligence Council under President Barack Obama.
Rumer told reporters in a briefing that the lack of sequencing speaks volumes and is a hallmark of Russian diplomacy which aims at “muddling any situation.”
It’s difficult to quibble with his pessimism. Russian President Vladimir Putin has a long track record of using peace talks to delay, obfuscate and exhaust opponents as he continues doing whatever he wants — all the while insisting that everything is interconnected and must be solved all at the same time.
Trying to solve everything means solving nothing. But then that’s the point. “It is obvious that Putin is simply stalling for time, trying to destroy or capture Ukraine or win this war of attrition, waiting for aid to stop in Europe and for Europe to be divided,” Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Mykola Kniazhytskyi told POLITICO.
The “let’s negotiate everything together” approach has been a key part of the playbook Putin and his Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov have used time and again when it comes to Ukraine, and earlier in Syria. Ukraine’s former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi, now his country’s ambassador to London, has been warning that it is designed to exhaust and wear down opponents and was also a classic Soviet ploy.
“Putin wants Empire, Ukrainians want freedom,” Kurt Volker, a former U.S. ambassador who served as a Special Representative for Ukraine Negotiations during Trump’s first term, told POLITICO.  “The rest is detail.” Assumptions that Putin wants peace, will negotiate seriously, or will accept a reasonable deal, “are all misguided,” he added.
Negotiations as a weapon of war can be used to distract, stall, allow time to maneuver and to ensnare the well-meaning — something that was highlighted between 2014 and 2017, when Lavrov and then U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry “negotiated” over Syria. The talks helped Moscow save Syria’s Bashar al-Assad from defeat, persuading then-president Obama to take his finger off the trigger and ignore his own red line on Damascus’ use of chemical weapons.
The only other top Kremlin aide as relentless as Lavrov in this technique of exhaustive obfuscation is Putin’s favorite “historian,” Vladimir Medinsky, who served as an arch-patriotic culture minister from 2012 to 2020. An advocate of putting up statues of Joseph Stalin, he has led the Russian delegation in talks with Ukraine stretching back to Istanbul in 2025. There he invoked the Great Northern War of 1700-21 as a warning that Russia is ready to fight Ukraine for as long as it takes to win. Medinsky again led the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi.
In fact, Moscow’s red lines have not shifted one iota in the years since Putin launched his full-scale invasion. The Russian leader and his top aides have emphatically outlined them for years — conditions that would, in effect, rip the nation of Ukraine to shreds. They want guarantees that Kyiv will never join NATO, that it will remain geopolitically neutral and unable to command its own fate, with severe limitations placed on stockpiles of weapons and the size of its army. Moscow also wants Crimea and the four eastern regions it claims as part of the Russian Federation to be internationally recognized as such.
And until then — as Medinsky has bragged — Russia will continue to wage war.

articles.title_orig: US urges owners of 720,000 BMW vehicles to park outside over fire risks
articles.title_zh: US urges owners of 720,000 BMW vehicles to park outside over fire risks
articles.content_orig:
Some of these cars and SUVs have been previously recalled for the same issue, which has to do with the water pump
BMW is recalling nearly three-quarters of a million cars and SUVs because an electrical connection may short-circuit and cause a fire.
If you own one of the following vehicles, federal safety regulators warn that you should park it outside until a recall repair is complete:
• 2012-2016 BMW 3 Series sedan
• 2012-2016 BMW 5 Series sedan
• 2012-2016 BMW Z4 convertible
• 2015-2016 BMW 4 Series Gran Coupe sedan
• 2015-2016 BMW 2 Series Convertible
• 2014-2016 BMW 328xi Gran Turismo sedan
• 2014-2016 BMW 2 Series Coupe
• 2014-2016 BMW 4 Series Convertible
• 2014-2016 BMW 3 Series Coupe
• 2014-2016 BMW 3 Series Wagon
• 2016-2018 BMW X5 xDrive40e SUV
Many of these vehicles have already been recalled for the same problem, but will need another trip to the dealership for a further fix.
According to documents that BMW shared with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the problem is due to an electrical connector on the vehicle’s water pump, which may allow moisture in. If this happens, the water pump could short-circuit and start a fire. So far, BMW says there have been 10 incidents related to this recall, but no crashes or injuries.
BMW is currently developing a fix for the problem and says that owners should expect two notices: One in December to let them know if their vehicle has been recalled, and another when a free fix is available at dealerships.
How to contact the manufacturer: Owners may contact BMW at 800-525-7417.
NHTSA campaign number: 26V733. It replaces recall 24V608.

Fire engulfed the Lukoil-owned Volgograd Oil Refinery following the overnight attack, according to eyewitness images and videos reviewed by the independent Russian outlet Astra. Regional Gov. Andrei Bocharov said that four employees in the cityâs southern industrial zone were killed and two others were injured.
Fire engulfed the Lukoil-owned Volgograd Oil Refinery, photos circulating on social. media show.
The refinery is among Russiaâs 10 largest, with capacity to process around 14 million tons of crude oil a yearâroughly 5 percent of the countryâs total refining capacity.
The attack came hours after U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff landed in Moscow on Thursday for fresh talks with Putin, as Trump seeks to put an end to the conflict that began nearly five years ago.
It also follows questions from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to the Trump administration about crippling disruptions to a military version of Elon Muskâs Starlink satellite network that Kyivâs military uses to intercept drones from Russia.

Bocharov said falling drone debris caused the blaze.
âAs a result of the drone debris falling, localized fires were recorded at a plant in Volgogradâs southern industrial zone, as well as in the adjacent area,â Bocharov said in a Telegram statement .
The attack delivers another blow to Putin as Kyiv r amps up its attacks on Russiaâs crucial energy infrastructure , more than four years into the war.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is battling a deepening fuel crisis as Ukraine batters his oil refineries.

Videos shared by Astra showed drivers lining up to refuel early on Friday morning.

The latest attack comes as Ukraine has struck nine of Russiaâs 35 major refineries since late October. Industry sources told Reuters that daily crude processing had fallen roughly 30 percent, from approximately 700,000 tons at the end of October to 500,000 by mid-November.
Putin had already threatened retaliation after earlier Ukrainian attacks on Russiaâs energy infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Why Jensen Huang’s Firing Couldn’t Happen To Mark Zuckerberg—Or Many Other Tech Titans
articles.title_zh: Why Jensen Huang’s Firing Couldn’t Happen To Mark Zuckerberg—Or Many Other Tech Titans
articles.content_orig:
MEDIA CONTACT: Ryon Harms, [email protected] , (310) 730-9407
EL CERRITO, CALIFORNIA — November 12, 2026 — NVIDIA’s board of directors today announced that CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following an independent board investigation. Huang, who founded and has led the company since 1993, allegedly put the company at risk of espionage through a recent affair. Because the Board is not handcuffed by dual class shares that insulate a reckless CEO, it has the power to weigh the situation and take action, a basic check on power that does not exist at Meta, SpaceX, and other companies including Anthropic and OpenAI that have planned IPOs built on dual class shares.
For As You Sow, the nation’s leading shareholder representative, the outcome shows corporate governance working as designed. NVIDIA has a single class of common stock. Every share carries one vote, shareholders elect the board, and the board can hold the CEO accountable for their actions. This chain of accountability is too often broken at public companies with dual-class shares.
“Even a founder who built one of the most valuable companies in the world needs accountability,” said Andrew Behar, CEO at As You Sow. “Leaders without guardrails can become reckless and put their company and shareholders at risk, we’ve seen this recently at Meta , a company facing potentially hundreds of billions of dollars of liability for actions that even company insiders called out as reckless, harmful, and addressable.”
For example, at Meta, Mark Zuckerberg holds roughly 61% of the company’s voting power, while owning only about 13% of the company, because each of his shares carries ten votes. SpaceX’s public offering gives Elon Musk and a small group of insiders ten-vote shares, with Musk serving as CEO, CTO, and board chair. Anthropic’s IPO filing shows its seven co-founders will control 50.1% of the vote, and OpenAI’s governance gives a nonprofit foundation the power to appoint and replace every director. In each case, control rests in one unaccountable person, or a small body of unaccountable people -- somewhere other than with the shareholders who own the company.
“When a founder controls the vote, the board serves at the founder’s pleasure, and its power to fire the CEO exists only on paper,” said Danielle Fugere, President & Chief Counsel As You Sow. “This builds inherent risk into a public company.”
In a September commentary in Fortune, As You Sow CEO Andrew Behar documented what that lack of oversight has cost at Meta: a settlement of up to $17.1 billion over claims that Facebook and Instagram were engineered to addict children, and another $25 billion settlement for lying about data privacy. As of December 2022, over 1,200 similar cases had been filed against Meta. In 2021, an As You Sowcontent governance resolution won 63.1% of Meta’s independent shareholder vote. Once Zuckerberg’s ten-to-one votes were counted, however, the reported result was only 19%. Many other shareholder proposals raising similar risks were filed at Meta.
An independent board with power to remove the CEO could not only assess this growing risk but taken action.  “NVIDIA’s board investigation that led to the resignation showed what true oversight looks like,” said Andrew Behar, CEO of As You Sow. “When a CEO takes imprudent action, there must be people in the boardroom with the authority to impose consequences. At NVIDIA, shareholders elect the board, and the board decides who runs the company. That’s how a public company is supposed to work.”
As You Sow has long advocated for one share, one vote at Meta and other dual-class companies, and will continue to press for governance structures that give shareholders a real voice and boards real authority.
As You Sow is the nation’s leading shareholder representative, with a 30+ year track record promoting environmental and social corporate responsibility. As You Sow addresses a range of issues that affect shareholder value including climate change, ocean plastics, toxins in the food system, biodiversity, racial justice, and workplace diversity. Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock slipped more than 4% on Friday as a sell-off in the semiconductor sector accelerated and investors digested the exit of Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chip heavyweight. The stock is expected to close out the week in the red, slipping below the $4 trillion market cap threshold. Some strategists point to a compelling valuation given Nvidia's forward PE (price-to-earnings) ratio of 13, with revenue growing at 60% year over year.
"We think the stock has support at $165 per share, and sentiment is extremely negative," said James Demmert, chief investment officer at Main Street Research, on Friday morning.
Shares of chipmakers AMD ( AMD ) dropped to session lows, sinking as much as 10%. Peers Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Intel ( INTC ) fell 6% and 5%, respectively.
Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ), which manufactures Nvidia chips, fell more than 3%. Semiconductor equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) was down 2%.
Storage maker Sandisk ( SNDK ) stock extended declines from the prior session, falling 9%. Shares of memory chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) also tanked 5% and 6%, respectively.

articles.title_orig: QSSR Upgrades Revealed For Six PS5 Games, Live Now in Marvel's Spider-Man 2
articles.title_zh: QSSR Upgrades Revealed For Six PS5 Games, Live Now in Marvel's Spider-Man 2
articles.content_orig:
As you may remember, QSSR is a new upscaling tech for the base PS5, built from the same "Project Amethyst" Sony and AMD collaboration that produced PSSR on PS5 Pro. Quick Spectral Super Resolution debuted on only two games - Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei - where we found it an impressive distillation of the AI upscaling tech that was well adapted for the more meagre hardware of the vanilla PS5, delivering better image quality and temporal stability than previous techniques like FSR or TSR. Now, QSSR has been announced for five more games, with Marvel's Spider-Man 2 leading the charge and debuting in a patch today.
Marvel's Wolverine proved the most impressive demonstration of QSSR thus far, so it will be fascinating to see how well it works in Marvel's Spider-Man 2 - which uses the same Insomniac Engine but crucially features a much wider open world. Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Insomniac, says that the team is "excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR's exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both fidelity and performance modes."
You'll have to wait a little longer to see QSSR in action in the other games mentioned in today's PlayStation blog , which comprise of Control Resonant, Arc Raiders, The Finals, No Man's Sky and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam. The latest Control title is set to get QSSR support next month, while the other titles promise the new technology either "soon" or "in the next few weeks".
You can click through to the blog to see a few side-by-sides that demonstrate the new technology in motion.
Of that list, I think I'm most excited to see QSSR in Hell Let Loose: Vietnam, as the game was widely panned for its image quality on launch, and QSSR ought to deliver a significant upgrade - though it may require a slightly lower base resolution, as we sometimes see with PSSR. It's a similar story in Control: Resonant, which could exhibit aliasing and artefacting in its performance mode .
The other three games - Arc Raiders, The Finals and No Man's Sky - have less pressinge image quality or stability concerns, but should still benefit from having the option of QSSR upscaling. It'll be interesting to see whether QSSR is offered as an option or whether it supplants existing solutions like FSR 3.
What games would be on your wishlist for QSSR upgrades on base PS5 - because of image quality issues, artefacting or other problems? Let me know in the comments below.

articles.title_orig: US Wholesale Inflation Picks Up to Fastest Pace Since 2022
articles.title_zh: US Wholesale Inflation Picks Up to Fastest Pace Since 2022
articles.content_orig:
Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.
The producer price index , which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.
On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.
The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.
Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.
Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.
The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.
However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.
"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.
Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.
"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."
Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.
Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.
Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."
Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

articles.title_orig: Man dies after eating bomb disguised as sweet dessert: ‘It exploded in his mouth’
articles.title_zh: Man dies after eating bomb disguised as sweet dessert: ‘It exploded in his mouth’
articles.content_orig:
An Indian man died Tuesday after eating an explosive that was disguised as a sweet dessert dumpling.
The 35-year-old victim, Rajendra Barautiya, had finished eating dinner with his family and was sitting by a bonfire outside his home when a neighbor handed him what appeared to be a rasgulla — a popular sweet made from cottage cheese, a ccording to India Today .
The supposed traditional treat was actually a ball of cheese dough filled with gunpowder, which is a trick used by villagers in Madhya Pradesh’s Dindori district to kill wild boars.
The bomb instantly detonated when Barautiya put it in his mouth, cops said.
“The bomb, used by some tribal people in the area to kill wild boars, was offered to this man,” police officer Rekha Singh told the AFP wire service. “It exploded in his mouth.”
Barautiya reportedly suffered severe injuries from the explosion and was rushed to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
A homicide case against the neighbor, Ram Bhagat Barotiya, and another man was pending and officials were looking into how he obtained the crude bomb and why he offered it to Rajendra, according to reports.
“We do not know whether the intention was to kill him or whether it was a malicious prank. That will be determined during the investigation,” Singh said.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo has made an emotional return to his former diocese of Chiclayo in Peru, where large crowds welcomed their former bishop exactly one month after he had lung cancer surgery, and he thanked them for their support during his recovery.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said.
About 500,000 people gathered for Mass at Pampas de Pimentel, a desert park just outside of Peru’s fourth-largest city, according to estimates from the Vatican, while another million lined his motorcade route.
Before he was elected pope, Leo had spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and served as bishop of Chiclayo, where he is still known as “Padre Roberto” and where his image is ubiquitous, from 2015 to 2023.
In Chiclayo, a coastal city of about 620,000, Leo earned a reputation for staying close to poor communities during times of crisis, including when the region was hit with devastating floods and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some had camped overnight to see him, while others walked in the hot sun to avoid bumper-to-bumper traffic to get to the open-air Mass.
As he rode in his popemobile, people in the crowd waved yellow and white Vatican flags and shouted, “The pope is from Chiclayo.”
“What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo,” said Leo at the start of his homily.
Originally from Chicago and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and declared the country his homeland on Wednesday.
Peru is the final stop of his 12-day, three-country South America tour, coming after visits to Argentina and Uruguay. Approximately 12 million people have come to see him at public events so far.
Last month, he underwent surgery for lung cancer, amid fears that the trip would have to be cancelled. But doctors have said the cancer was localised, had not spread, and would not require further treatment .
Leo will stay in the Chiclayo area until Sunday, leading eight events, including a private dinner with the priests he oversaw during his time as bishop.

articles.title_orig: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation
articles.title_zh: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation
articles.content_orig:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.
"I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility," the policymaker said during an interview on "Squawk Box."
His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index , considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.
With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," he said.
"Inflation is rising. It's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we're adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it's starting to spread out of its lane," Goolsbee added.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week's inflation data.
Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.
"It's it's all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?" he said. "My feeling is, right now we're not."

articles.title_orig: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.
Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.
Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."
Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.
There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.
Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.
Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

articles.title_orig: Watch CNBC's full interview with Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent on Nvidia, China trade
articles.title_zh: Watch CNBC's full interview with Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent on Nvidia, China trade
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal.
But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."
The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.
Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.

articles.title_orig: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.title_zh: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.content_orig:
Police forces, hospitals, GP surgeries and councils across the south of England have been sharing advice and updates after a global Microsoft outage left them without email access.
Most say they are continuing to operate as normal but some online forms and electronic-based services are not working and there may be delays to enquiries.
The region's three police forces - Hampshire & Isle of Wight, Thames Valley and Dorset - all said their phone lines were working and they were able to respond to emergencies but their online reporting systems were down.
Hospitals have asked outpatients to attend booked appointments, adding there was no need to check they were going ahead.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems" .
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues on Friday had so far been unsuccessful.
In a Facebook update on Friday morning, Dorset Police said: "We are currently unable to receive online form submissions. Until this is resolved, if your report is time-critical but not an emergency, please dial 101.
"If your report can wait until Microsoft restores its service, please submit an online form once you are able to do so."
Hampshire police sought to allay fears about the effect of the outage on services.
It said: "We can confirm that our ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls has not been impacted by the widely reported issues with Microsoft.
"We know that the current situation will be causing concern... but our ability to respond to emergencies has not been compromised."
Isle of Wight NHS Trust said its emergency services remained operational through the outage and teams had "established plans in place to minimise disruption and maintain safe patient care".
It said: "If your enquiry is urgent, please contact the relevant service by telephone rather than email where possible."
Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said: "Our services remain operational, but there may be delays in responding to enquiries.
"If you need to contact us, please telephone us rather than email.
"If you have an appointment with us, please attend as planned. There is no need to contact us to confirm your appointment."
Tower House GP surgery in Ryde said the outage could affect some of its services, with delays responding to online consultations, hospital letters and discharge documents.
It said it was prioritising urgent clinical matters and patient safety.
Slough Borough Council in Berkshire said staff at its customer service centre who usually dealt with email enquiries had been transferred onto the phones but urged people only to call if their request was urgent because lines were expected to be busy.
East Hampshire District Council said its emails were down but residents registered on its MyEHDC system could still use the general enquiries form.
Lyme Regis Town Council in Dorset said it was using a mobile phone number for urgent issues because its telephone lines were also affected and working intermittently.

articles.title_orig: Apple should have made the MacBook logo RGB
articles.title_zh: Apple should have made the MacBook logo RGB
articles.content_orig:
The PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.
The PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.
When Apple CEO John Ternus announced the first touchscreen Mac last month, the biggest reaction in the room wasn’t for the PROLED MacBook Pro ’s OLED touchscreen or the thinner and lighter chassis; it was for the illuminated lid logo. It’s a throwback to the light-up logos on the old MacBooks, which Apple started phasing out in 2015 , and which were completely gone by the 2018 MacBook Air redesign . It’s a nostalgia play, but boy did it work. It’s fun!
Just like in the old days, the new logo’s brightness is linked to the screen’s: The brighter or dimmer the screen, the brighter or dimmer the logo. But the light-up logo on the old MacBooks was illuminated by the screen’s backlight, and an OLED display doesn’t have one. Thanks to iFixit , we now know it’s lit by four white LEDs and synced with the screen’s brightness by software. But that means Apple could have used RGB LEDs.
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, or anything in between? On the lid of your new MacBook Pro? Why not? After all, Apple insists it’s still serious about gaming , and nothing says “serious about gaming” like RGB lighting.
I was secretly hoping users would be able to customize the illuminated lid cutout much like the Xbox logo on Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 controllers . But alas, no luck. You can turn off the illumination with some Terminal commands or take control of it with a third-party app. But when it’s lit, it’s only lit with white light. And iFixit’s teardown also showed the difficulty of accessing those LEDs (the screen delaminated and broke in the process). So we’re unlikely to see LED RGB mods for it unless someone’s brave enough to void their warranty and risk a pricey screen repair on their $3,000 laptop.
The most fun you can have with the Apple lid logo is to install a free third-party app like LogoLight and have it pulse, breathe, match the beat of any music you’re playing, or flash some Morse code. There’s some fun there, but if you combined these features with a splash of color we’d really be cooking.
MacBooks aren’t gaming laptops, so RGB lighting may seem like a mismatch, but multicolor LEDs could have been a cool Easter egg. Nobody thought Apple would put a touchscreen on a MacBook either, and the iPhone Duo and HomeView also show Apple is in a new age of experimentation during the early Ternus era. Maybe if the light-up lid logo ever comes to future MacBook Airs or a MacBook Neo, Apple could cut loose a little.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.
On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt  lingers.
It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.
Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.
It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.
"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.
"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."
"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."
Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.
The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."
— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.
